## Methods

Study approval
BC tissues samples were gathered from female patients with breast cancer at the Women's Hospital of Nanjing Medical University. Informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to sample collection, including consent to publish potentially identifying clinical information. The Clinical Research Ethics Committee of the Women’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University granted the study protocol, ensuring adherence to ethical standards. Animal experiments were conducted in accordance with protocols approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of Nanjing Medical University, which sets a maximum allowable tumor size of 225 mm². Mice that exceeded this limit were humanely euthanized and used for subsequent in vitro analyses.

Human samples
BC tissues were obtained from 30 randomly selected female patients (See Supplementary Table 1) in Women's Hospital of Nanjing Medical University, with informed consent achieved from all patients. Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes were isolated and concentrated via density-gradient centrifugation with Lymphoprep (78071, Stem cell). DCs were enriched via the Human Pan-DC Pre-Enrichment Kit (19521, Stem cell). The enriched DCs were treated with the indicated drugs and subsequently lysed for protein and RNA extraction for downstream analyses. This study was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Nanjing Women and Children's Healthcare Hospital (Approval No. 2024KY-137-01). All participants provided written informed consent prior to enrollment and did not receive financial compensation. All samples were collected and used exclusively for scientific research purposes in accordance with the approved ethical guidelines.

Mice
All mice strains were maintained with a C57BL/6 background. G6pdx-floxed mice (Cyagen) were crossed with Zbtb46-Cre mice (Shanghai Model Organisms) to generate G6pdx+/+Zbtb46-Cre mice and G6pdx fl/flZbtb46-Cre mice. Tmem173-/- mice (STING deficient) (Shanghai Model Organisms) crossed with G6pdxfl/flZbtb46-Cre mice to obtain G6pdxfl/flZbtb46-Cre Tmem173-/- mice. All mice used in our experiments were 6-12-week-old gender-matched mice. Both male and female mice were included to avoid sex bias. All mice were housed in a specific pathogen-free (SPF) facility at the Animal Core Facility of Nanjing Medical University under a standard 12-hour light/dark cycle, with ambient temperature maintained at 22 ± 1 °C and relative humidity at 50 ± 10%.

Cell lines and cell culture
DC2.4 (murine dendritic cells, SCC142) was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. MC38 (murine colon cancer, ENH204-FP) was obtained from Kerafast. LLC (murine Lewis lung carcinoma, CRL-1642), B16-F10 (murine melanoma, CRL-6475), and HEK293T (human embryonic kidney cells, CRL-3216) were obtained from ATCC. LLC, MC38, and HEK293T cells were maintained in DMEM supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin. DC2.4 and B16-F10 cells were cultured in RPMI 1640 medium containing 10% FBS and 1% penicillin/streptomycin.

BMDC generation and culture
Bone marrow cells were extracted from tibiae and femurs of mice and subjected to treatment with red blood cell lysis buffer. The cells were then cultured for 7 days in RPMI 1640 medium containing 200 ng/mL FLT-3L (BE0098, Bio X Cell), 10% FBS and 1% penicillin/streptomycin to generate BMDCs. Live CD11c+MHC-II+ cells were isolated by flow cytometry for further experiments.

Cell isolation
Single-cell suspensions of the spleen were prepared for cell isolation. Splenic DCs (Spl-DC) were isolated utilizing the Mouse CD11c Positive Selection Kit (18780, Stem Cell). For tumor samples, tissues were enzymatically digested, followed by density-gradient centrifugation with Percoll (Cytiva) to enrich TILs. Tumor-infiltrating DCs (Tu-DC) were isolated via flow cytometry by gating on CD45+CD24-F4/80-Ly6C-CD11c+MHC-II+ cells.

Flow cytometry
Single-cell suspensions were prepared for flow cytometry analysis. For surface marker analysis, cells were incubated with specific fluorochrome-labeled antibodies in MACS buffer (PBS supplemented with 2% FBS and 1 mM EDTA) for 30 minutes following by flow cytometry analysis. For intracellular staining, cells were labeled with surface marker antibodies and then fixed with fixation/permeabilization buffer at 4°C for 1 hour. Subsequently, the cells were labeled with the relevant fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies in permeabilization buffer. To evaluate intracellular cytokine production, the cells underwent stimulation with phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA), monensin and ionomycin for 4 hours, then harvested and incubated with appropriate fluorochrome-labeled antibodies for flow cytometry analysis.

Co-culture assay of OT-I T cells with DCs
OT-I T cells were isolated from the spleens of OT-I mice using the Mouse CD8 Positive Selection Kit (18953, Stem Cell). OT-II T cells were isolated from the spleens of OT-II mice using the Mouse CD4 T cell Isolation Kit (480033, Biolegend). For the detection of T cell expansion, 1x105 OT-I or OT-II T cells were labeled with CFSE (C34570, Thermo Fisher Scientific), then co-cultured with 3x104 DCs and supplemented with SIINFEKL peptides (A5503, Sigma) for 72 hours. The proliferation of T cells was analyzed via CFSE dilution using flow cytometry. To assess cell proliferation and effector cytokine expression of T cells, 1x105 OT-I or OT-II T cells were incubated with 3x104 DCs in the presence of SIINFEKL peptide for 72 hours, and the proportions of T cells producing Ki-67, GZMB, IFN- and TNF- were determined by flow cytometry.

Western blot
2x106 Cell pellets were gathered and then resuspended in the lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, and 1 mM EDTA, supplemented with phosphatase and protease inhibitor cocktails) at 4℃ for 20 minutes. The cell extracts were then centrifuged at 4°C for 10 minutes. After centrifugation, the supernatants resulting from the separation were collected for subsequent western blot analysis.

RNA extraction and qRT-PCR
Total RNA was extracted utilizing TRIzol Reagent (AG21102, Accurate Biology). Subsequently, cDNA was generated utilizing the one-step RT-gDNA digestion SuperMix for qPCR (11142ES60, YEASEN). The qRT-PCR was performed with specific primers as detailed in Supplementary Table 2, coupled with qPCR SYBR Green Master Mix (11202ES60, YEASEN).

RNA sequencing
For smart-RNA sequencing, tumor-infiltrating cDCs were isolated and purified via flow cytometry. Total RNA was enriched utilizing TRIzol Reagent and sequenced on the Illumina NovaSeq™ 6000 platform to acquire 150bp paired-end reads. Subsequent mapping to the Mus musculus reference genome (mm10) was achieved using HISAT2. GSEA software facilitated GSEA analysis, and KEGG pathway enrichment analysis was utilized by clusterProfiler. The RNA sequencing data have been uploaded to the Genome Sequence Archive of the National Genomics Data Center, available at https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/gsa/search?searchTerm=CRA020726 (accession numbers: CRA020726).

Signal-cell RNA sequencing
For single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), tumor-infiltrating DCs were harvested from MC38 tumor-bearing mice. Transcriptomic profiling was conducted using the BD Rhapsody system. scRNA-seq libraries were constructed following the BD Rhapsody single-cell whole-transcriptome amplification workflow and sequenced utilizing DNBSEQ-T7 for 150 bp paired-end reads. Data analysis was proceeded in R (v4.4.0) via a Seurat (v5.1.0) pipeline. Cells displaying > 20% mitochondrial gene expression and > 5000 detected genes were filtered out. Clustering was done using the FindClusters() function with a resolution of 0.5. High lineage marker-expressing cell clusters (Cd3d, Cd19, Ncr1, Adgre1) were excluded. To investigate the potential function of cDCs, we further distinguished cDCs subpopulations (identified by Itgax, Flt3 and Zbtb46) from total DCs. Differential gene expression within specific clusters was explored with the FindMarkers() function, employing a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test by default. The RNA sequencing data have been uploaded to the Genome Sequence Archive of the National Genomics Data Center, available at https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/gsa/search?searchTerm=CRA017022 (accession numbers: CRA017022).

Metabolite extraction and mass spectrometry
2x106 late- and early-stage intratumoral cDCs (live CD45+CD24-F4/80-Ly6C-CD11c+MHC-II+) were isolated by flow cytometry from MC38 inoculated wild-type mice. Cell pellet was collected by centrifuging at 100 × g and 4 ℃ for 5 minutes. Samples were mixed with 500 µL extraction buffer (methanol: water = 3:1, containing 0.5×internal standard). After placement on dry ice for pre-cooling, the samples underwent three freeze-thaw cycles in liquid nitrogen, followed by vortexing for 30 s to mix well. Subsequent sonication was performed in an ice-water bath for 15 minutes, and samples were then incubated at -40 °C for 1 hours. Following centrifugation at 13800 × g and 4 °C for 15 minutes, 200 µL of supernatant was collected into a 2.0 mL tube and dried under vacuum. The dried residue was then reconstituted in 160 µL of methanol: acetonitrile: water (1:1:2, v/v/v). The solution was filtered and placed into an autosampler vial for liquid chromatography-high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC-MS). For reversed-phase system, an Agilent 1290 UPLC system equipped with an ACQUITY UPLC BEH C18 column (1.7 µm, 2.1 × 150 mm) was used. For hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography (HILIC) system, the same UPLC system was employed with an Atlantis Premier BEH Z-HILIC column (1.7 µm, 2.1 × 150 mm). An AB Sciex Triple Quad 6500+ mass spectrometer was used for metabolite detection. Raw LC-MS/MS data were processed using SCIEX Analyst Workstation Software (v1.7.3), and metabolite quantification was performed with the automated analysis software BIOTREE Bio Bud (v2.0.3)

DC stimulation and drug treatment
DC2.4, BMDCs and tumor-infiltrating DCs were quantified and then seeded into designated cell culture plates. To trigger STING signaling in DC2.4 and BMDCs, the cells were subjected to treatment with ISD, cGAMP or DMXAA for 4 hours. ISD and cGAMP were transfected utilizing PEI (40815ES03, YEASEN) transfection reagent. DCs were treated with MITO-TEMPO (20 μM), R5P (200 μM), AG1 (3 μM), G6PDi-1 (100 μM), 6-AN (50 μM), 6-MP (50 μM), 5-FU (10 μM), LEF (50 μM) or BRQ (1 μM) for 12 hours and then harvested for further experiments. The ISD used in this study was prepared with equimolar amounts of oligonucleotides: F: 5′-TACAGATCTACTAGTGATCTATGACTGATCTGTACATGATCTACATACAGATCTACTAGTGATCTATGACTGATCTGTACATGATCTACA-3′; R: 5′-TGTAGATCATGTACAGATCAGTCATAGATCACTAGTAGATCTGTATGTAGATCATGTACAGATCAGTCATAGATCACTAGTAGATCTGTA-3′. The oligonucleotides were annealed in PBS at 70℃ for 30 minutes before cooling to room temperature.

Nucleotides supplement assay
BMDCs were pre-treated with ATP (100 μM) and GTP (100 μM) for 4 hours, followed by treatment with the corresponding drugs for 12 hours. Subsequently, the quantified cells were plated into specified cell culture plates and stimulated with ISD for 4 hours before being harvested for subsequent experiments. Tumor-infiltrating DCs were counted and then seeded into designated cell culture plates. After pre-treatment with ATP and GTP for 12 hours, the cells were collected for further investigations.

ATP, GTP and cGAMP measurement
To measure ATP levels, 3x105 cells were plated in the 12-well cell culture plate, and the intracellular ATP levels were detected by the Luminescent Cell Viability Assay (G7570, Promega) in accordance with the instructions of manufacturer. For GTP and cGAMP measurements, 1x106 cell pellets were lysed in Protein Extraction Reagent (78503, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Subsequently, the cell lysates were utilized for assessing intracellular GTP levels and cGAMP levels using the GTP ELISA Kit (66393A, MEIBIAO BIOLOGY) and the 2’3’-cGAMP ELISA Kit (501700, Cayman Chemical) respectively, according to the instructions of manufacturer.

Stable cell lines generation
Mouse G6pdx was cloned into the MSCV2.2 plasmids. HEK293T cells were transfected with MSCV2.2-G6PDX plasmid in conjunction with pge plasmid to generate lentivirus. After 48 hours, the supernatants containing the lentivirus were collected. DC2.4 cells were then exposed to the lentivirus-containing supernatants with polybrene (10 μg/mL) for 12 hours. Subsequently, the medium was refreshed for another 12 hours, repeating this cycle. The transduced G6PDX-overexpressing cells (GFP+) were isolated using flow cytometry for subsequent experiments.

Tumor model
Tumor size, calculated as length × width (mm²), served as an indicator of tumor growth. Tumor-induced lethality was defined as a tumor reaching 225 mm². For the subcutaneous tumor model, MC38 (5x105 cells per mouse), B16-F10 (1x106 cells per mouse) and LLC (1x106 cells per mouse) were injected subcutaneously into G6pdx+/+Zbtb46-Cre and G6pdxfl/flZbtb46-Cre mice. For the BMDC-based therapeutic tumor model, wild-type mice were injected subcutaneously of MC38-OVA (5x105 cells per mouse) tumor cells. On day 3 and day 6 post tumor cell inoculation, the mice were subcutaneously injected adjacent to the tumors with BMDCs (3x106 cells per mouse) that had been pre-treated with SIINFEKL peptides (A5503, Sigma) overnight. For another DC-based therapy tumor model, MC38 (5x105 cells per mouse) tumor-bearing wild-type mice (on day 6 post tumor cell inoculation) were subcutaneously injected adjacent to the tumors with 3x106 intratumoral cDCs. Early- and late-stage intratumoral cDCs were isolated from wild-type MC38 tumor-bearing mice (5×10⁵ cells per mouse) at day 10 and day 20 post-inoculation, respectively. Intratumoral cDCs (live CD45+CD24-F4/80-Ly6C-CD11c+MHC-II+) cells were isolated by flow cytometry. For in vitro treatment, early-stage intratumoral cDCs were treated with PPP inhibitors (G6PDi-1 or 6-AN) or untreated (Ctrl) for 12 hours, and late-stage intratumoral cDCs were treated with the PPP agonist AG1 or untreated (Ctrl) for 12 hours prior to subcutaneous injection. For the combined anti-PD-L1 therapeutic tumor model, wild-type mice received an injection of MC38-OVA (5x105 cells per mouse) tumor cells and treated with anti-PD-L1 antibodies or IgG2b isotype control (100 ug per mouse) every 3 days for a total of three doses. Additionally, AG1-treated or non-treated BMDCs (3x106 cells per mouse), pre-incubated with SIINFEKL peptides overnight, were subcutaneously injected adjacent to the tumors on days 3 and 6 post-tumor inoculation.

Quantification and statistical analysis
Statistical analysis was carried out utilizing GraphPad Prism 8.0 software, with results presented as mean ± SEM. Two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-tests were utilized to assess parameters between two distinct groups. One-way ANOVA was employed to analyze the comparisons involving more than two groups with a single variable. Two-way ANOVA analyses were conducted for comparing multiple experimental groups or continuous outcomes. Survival curves underwent assessment via the log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test. Gene expression levels from scRNA-seq data were examined using a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript by Liu investigates how tumor immunoediting affects DC function, focusing on the role of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP). Using single-cell analysis and functional assays, the authors report that late-stage tumor–infiltrating DCs exhibit reduced PPP activity, which compromises their antitumor capacity. Mechanistically, PPP-driven purine metabolism is proposed to sustain cGAS–STING signaling and thereby promote DC-mediated immune responses. The study suggests PPP as an intrinsic metabolic checkpoint of DC function and a potential therapeutic target to enhance immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). This work addresses an important question at the intersection of tumor immunology and immunometabolism, and the link between PPP and STING signaling is intriguing. However, several aspects of the data presentation and mechanistic claims require clarification and further support.
Major Comments
1. The study demonstrates that PPP deficiency leads to DC dysfunction, while pharmacological or genetic activation of the PPP only modestly restores DC function. This suggests that PPP is necessary but may not be sufficient for full DC activation. The authors should clarify this point and discuss whether direct STING agonist treatment might represent a more effective strategy than PPP augmentation.
2. In Figure 4L, it remains unclear whether STING agonists retain their ability to activate DCs in PPP-deficient conditions or PPP knockout mice. Testing this point would clarify whether PPP is strictly upstream of STING signaling or acts in parallel.
3. In Supplementary Figure 6, the use of 6-MP shows that purine metabolism is required for STING signaling. However, no data are provided on whether supplementing R5P can restore signaling. Without this, the claim that“PPP- driving purine metabolism boosts STING signaling”might be overstated. Rescue experiments or a toned-down interpretation is needed.
4. In Figure 6A, the model suggests that reduced PPP activity limits ATP/GTP production and thereby compromises DC function. If so, supplementation with ATP/GTP in wild-type DCs at late tumor stages should alleviate dysfunction. The lack of such an effect requires explanation.
5. Tumor growth curves across treatment groups appear modest and could be problematic, dose and timing optimization for better therapeutic effects? To better illustrate therapeutic effects, the authors should provide individual tumor growth trajectories in addition to group averages.
6. While PPP activation is proposed to synergize with ICB, the therapeutic benefit appears modest. Stronger preclinical evidence or more nuanced discussion of clinical implications might be helpful to understand whole picture.
Minor Comments
1. Figure 2D, 2H, S2B, S2C, S2F, S2G, S8A-C: The data presentation is not appropriate. The authors normalized all values by dividing by 10³, which obscures the actual magnitude of differences. It would be more informative to present the raw MFI values directly and then assess the differences between groups accordingly. Please revise the figure and reanalyze the data.
2. In Figure 4D, the actin loading control appears inconsistent across samples, which raises concerns about normalization. The authors should clarify or provide quantification to ensure reliability of the results.
3. In Figure 6B, DC numbers are presented without accounting for differences in tumor size. Normalization to tumor weight (e.g., DCs per gram tumor) would allow more accurate comparisons.

### Reviewer 2

In the manuscript “Tumor immunoediting shapes pentose phosphate pathway to dictate DC function”, Liu et al. demonstrate that late-stage tumors exhibit reduced pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) activity, which correlates with a diminished ability to activate T cells within the tumor. Their findings suggest that the tumor microenvironment suppresses PPP activity, which is essential for fueling purine metabolism and providing ATP and GTP for 2’3’-cGAMP synthesis and cGAS activity. Reduced PPP activity ultimately leads to impaired cGAS signaling in dendritic cells and decreased expression of type I interferon genes.
The concept of the manuscript is well formulated, and the in vitro experiments using bone marrow–derived dendritic cells to show how PPP activity supports cGAS activation were interesting and well executed. However, the in vivo results that form the basis of the authors’ hypothesis and subsequent experiments lack critical controls and fail to account for the functional diversity of dendritic cells, which varies by origin (type 1 or type 2 DC) and maturation state (e.g., CCR7⁺ DCs). Although the authors performed single-cell RNA sequencing of dendritic cells and highlighted their heterogeneity, all in vivo experiments were conducted on total dendritic cells. This is problematic because CCR7⁺ mature dendritic cells are known to be the primary subset capable of activating T cells in tumors, and DC1 and DC2 populations differ in their ability to cross-present antigens.
Below are specific comments to improve and strengthen the manuscript:
Major Points
• Figure 1: The metabolomics assay is not described in the Materials and Methods section. How was it performed on tumor-infiltrating DCs? Without this information, it is difficult to interpret the results—specifically, the number and type of cells analyzed.
• How did the authors define the DC population in the single-cell dataset? Can they compare their data to publicly available dendritic cell signatures? How do they explain the absence of mature DCs in their single-cell analysis?
• If different DC subsets were identified in the single-cell data, why were subsequent analyses performed on total DCs? Why were maturation markers and cytokines assessed in immature DCs rather than focusing on mature CCR7⁺ DCs?
• Figure 1: Why did the authors validate the single-cell data using qPCR? Can they validate CCR7 expression at the protein level? Does the downregulation of maturation genes indicate fewer mature DCs in the tumor or reduced protein levels within mature DCs?
• The GSEA was performed on total DCs. Could the authors identify mature DCs in the single-cell dataset and perform GSEA specifically on this population, which is responsible for T-cell activation?
• For KEGG pathway analysis, it would be important to determine whether mature DCs exhibit lower PPP activity.
• Figure 2: The authors treated tumors with PPP inhibitors and assessed maturation markers. Instead, could they quantify the proportion of mature CCR7⁺ DCs and measure the gMFI of maturation markers in this subset?
• Figure 2: The description of how tumor DCs were recovered, stimulated, and re-injected is unclear. Were these total DCs? Were mature DCs excluded? Were DC1 and DC2 subsets considered? What was the viability of these cells after sorting and 12-hour in vitro stimulation prior to re-injection?
• Related to the previous point: Did the treatment induce maturation of immature DCs in vitro? How were injected and non-injected tumor DCs distinguished for comparison? The experimental design is not well explained. Were control samples injected with untreated tumor DCs recovered and re-injected after 12 hours? Did the treatment itself alter maturation markers before injection?
• Still in Figure 2: When augmenting PPP activity, the authors assessed maturation markers by qPCR in total DCs. Could they instead quantify mature DCs in the tumor and measure gMFI of maturation and activation markers? It is difficult to conclude that PPP activity impacts DC maturation and activation based solely on RNA levels in total DCs.
• Figure 3: Could the authors quantify mature DCs in tumors from G6pdx⁺/⁺ Zbtb46-Cre (WT) and KO mice? Also, assess immature DC1 and DC2 infiltration to determine whether KO DCs have reduced tumor infiltration capacity.
• Figure 4: The rationale for injecting G6pdx⁺/⁺ Zbtb46-Cre (WT) and KO BMDCs into tumors and monitoring tumor growth is unclear. If the tumor microenvironment impairs PPP activity in DCs, why would WT BMDCs be unaffected? Wouldn’t WT BMDCs also experience PPP suppression? Please clarify.
• What is ISD, which was used to stimulate BMDCs?
• Figure 4J: The rationale for comparing tumor growth after injection of WT versus STING-pathway KO BMDCs is unclear. How do the authors explain that injected BMDCs promote tumor growth compared to WT BMDCs? Please comment.
• Figure 6: Does treatment with ATP and GTP induce maturation in KO DCs? Is the observed effect due to injecting mature BMDCs? Why is there no effect in WT BMDCs treated with ATP and GTP? The lack of tumor growth reduction in WT suggests that supplementation is insufficient to overcome PPP deficiency. How do the authors explain that KO BMDCs promote tumor growth and that supplementation restores tumor growth to WT levels?
• Do KO BMDCs become more immunosuppressive in the tumor compared to WT BMDCs?

### Reviewer 3

Several studies in pre-clinical models have demonstrated an indespensible role for conventional dendritic cells (cDCs), particularly cDC1s, in promoting T cell responses to cancer and augmenting the efficacy of T cell‐based immunotherapies. While the link between cancer immunity and cDCs has been extensively studied, there is now growing interest in understanding the cel intrinsic determinants of cDC that govern cDC function.
Work from Liu et al. reports cDC metabolism as a key component of their anti-tumour activity. The authors showed that the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) is essential for cDC activation and their capacity to prime T cells. Although PPP activity is evident in intratumoural cDCs at early stages, it becomes suppressed during later stages of tumour progression, thereby contributing to immune evasion. Using conditional knockout mouse models and ex vivo/in vitro assays, the authors further showed that PPP deficiency compromises STING phosphorylation and downstream signalling. Pharmacological activation of the PPP restores antitumor immunity and enhances the efficacy of immune checkpoint blocakde. Finally, analysis of human breast cancer samples reveals that the expression of key PPP enzymes correlates with signatures of intratumoral cDC accumulation. While the mechanism proposed by the authors meets the novelty criteria expected for publication in Nature Communications and the experiments are generally well designed, the following points need to be addressed to improve the clarity and overall quality of the manuscript.
Major points:
- It would be important to clarify whether the cDC1/cDC2 ratio is maintained between early- and late-stage tumours. If this is not the case, it becomes difficult to draw firm conclusions from the T cell activation assays, as the observed differences in ex vivo T cell priming could result either from functional impairment of cDC subsets or from numerical differences in cDC1 and cDC2 populations between early and late tumours. The authors should therefore normalise the T cell activation assays based on the cDC1/cDC2 ratio to ensure comparability between the groups.
- In Figure 1, it would be important to determine whether the activation of both cDC subsets (cDC1 and cDC2) as well as their ability to prime T cells are equally affected by the suppression of PPP-pathway in late tumours. Identifying which subset is primarily impacted would enhance the mechanistic understanding of this study. To this end, the authors should repeat the T cell activation assays using separately purified cDC1 and cDC2 populations.
- In Figures 3E and F, the appropriate control for G6pdxfl/flZbtb46Cre mice is G6pdxfl/fl; the authors should repeat the tumour growth profile using this control line for accurate comparison. Alternatively, the authors could provide tumour growth data of WT, Zbtb46Cre and G6pdxfl/fl within the same experiment to demonstrate that tumour progression is comparable across these lines and that they can be used interchangeably.
- Given that PPP-deficient cDCs show impaired ability to prime antigen-specific T cells, it would be important to clarify whether the tumour growth retardation observed in mice with enhanced cDC PPP activity is CD8⁺ T cell-dependent. The authors could address this by depleting CD8⁺ T cells using specific antibodies in mice adoptively transferred with cDCs exhibiting enhanced PPP activity.
Minor but essential points:
- Figure legends should be revised for clarity and completeness, explicitly stating the number and type of replicates in each panel (e.g., whether each point in the graphs represents a biological or technical replicate).
- The statement on lines 152–153 “Consistent with the metabolic profiling, late-stage intratumoral cDCs exhibited markedly decreased NADPH and R5P production (Figure 2B)." is not adequately supported by data and should be revised or removed.
- The authors should clearly define every gene, abbreviation, and mouse model used in the figures and main text. For example, specify which protein is absent in TmemKO mice. Figure legends should be self-explanatory and allow readers to interpret the data without referring to the methods section.
Similarly, in figure 5 and 6, please clarify in the panels the exact genotypes of the WT and KO mice.
- The combination “A + G + ISD” requires clarification. The authors should specify in both the main text and figure legend what each acronym represents and briefly describe the mechanism of action (text and methods) of these STING agonists, particularly in contrast to the other cGAS/STING agonists used elsewhere in the manuscript.
- It would be interesting to investigate whether a high PPP-related gene signature enhances the predictive value of the cDC1 gene signature (e.g. comparing patients with high PPP/high cDC1, low PPP/high cDC1, low PPP/low cDC1, high PPP/low cDC1 expression). The authors could analyse some of the TCGA datasets previously used to show that intratumoral cDC1 gene signatures positively correlate with patient survival, as reported by JP Böttcher etal., 2018 (DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2018.01.004 )
- The title should be changed and refined based on the data the authors have provided. There is no experimental evidence for tumour immunoediting – immunoediting refers historically to the experiments that have been conducted by R D Schreiber’s group, none of which are listed in this manuscript.
