Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s helpful comments and comprehensive consideration of our manuscript. To address these comments, we treated wild-type (WT) and G6pdx-KO (PPP deficient) BMDCs with R5P. We observed that PPP deficiency markedly suppressed STING signaling. Supplementation with R5P restored both STING activation and downstream type I interferons production (Supplemental Figure 7, g and h). These results confirm that PPP impairment disrupts purine synthesis by limiting R5P availability, thereby inhibiting STING signaling in DCs.
4. In Figure 6A, the model suggests that reduced PPP activity limits ATP/GTP production and thereby compromises DC function. If so, supplementation with ATP/GTP in wild-type DCs at late tumor stages should alleviate dysfunction. The lack of such an effect requires explanation.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for your valuable comments. In accordance with the suggestion, we isolated late-stage tumor-infiltrating DCs from MC38 tumor-bearing wild-type mice and treated them in vitro with ATP and GTP for 12h. Supplementation with ATP and GTP restored the expression of key maturation markers including MHC-I, CD80, and CD86 in late-stage intratumoral DCs to levels comparable to early-stage intratumoral DCs (Supplemental Figure 8h). Correspondingly, qPCR analysis confirmed that ATP and GTP supplementation also rescued the expression of functional cytokines in late-stage intratumoral DCs (Supplemental Figure 8i). Taken together, these findings demonstrate that PPP dysfunction in late-stage intratumoral DCs disrupts purine metabolism, resulting in diminished ATP and GTP levels that contribute to functional impairment. Importantly, supplementation with ATP and GTP effectively rescues the functional capacity of late-stage intratumoral DCs.
5. Tumor growth curves across treatment groups appear modest and could be problematic, dose and timing optimization for better therapeutic effects? To better illustrate therapeutic effects, the authors should provide individual tumor growth trajectories in addition to group averages.
Response: We thank the reviewer for your valuable comments. In accordance with the suggestion to enhance tumor therapeutic efficacy, we had modified the treatment protocol by initiating PD-L1 administration at an earlier timepoint and incorporating an increased dose of AG1. The updated experimental scheme, now included in the revised manuscript as follows: “For the combined anti-PD-L1 and AG1 therapeutic tumor model, wild-type mice were received an injection of MC38-OVA (5x105 cells per mouse) tumor cells and treated with anti-PD-L1 antibodies (100 μg per mouse) at days 6, 9 and 12 post-tumor inoculation for a total of three doses. Additionally, AG1-treated (4 μM) or non-treated BMDCs (3x106 cells per mouse), pre-incubated with OVA overnight, were subcutaneously injected adjacent to the tumors on days 3 and 6 post-tumor inoculation.”
We observed that anti-PD-L1 antibody treatment or AG1 stimulation alone resulted in reduced tumor size (Figure 6i and Supplemental Figure 9d). Notably, combining anti-PD-L1 antibody with AG1 led to a significant reduction in tumor size (Figure 6i and Supplemental Figure 9d), accompanied by increased populations of CD11c+ lymphocytes, CD4+ T, and CD8+ T cells (Figure 6j), along with higher frequencies of IFN-- and TNF--producing CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Figure 6, k and l) in the TME. To better illustrate the therapeutic efficacy, we had included individual tumor growth curves in Supplemental Figure 9d. These data clearly show that the combination of anti-PD-L1 antibody and AG1 results in the smallest tumor volumes among all treatment groups.
6. While PPP activation is proposed to synergize with ICB, the therapeutic benefit appears modest. Stronger preclinical evidence or more nuanced discussion of clinical implications might be helpful to understand whole picture.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this constructive feedback, which has significantly strengthened our study.
First, in response to the observation that the efficacy of the ICB and AG1 combination was modest, we had optimized the treatment protocol by initiating anti-PD-L1 administration earlier and increasing the AG1 dosage. This revised strategy achieved the strongest antitumor effect among all treatment groups (Figure 6, i-l, and Supplemental Figure 9d). These results provide stronger preclinical evidence that PPP activation can effectively synergize with ICB.
Second, we fully agree that a more in-depth discussion of the clinical implications of PPP activation for tumor therapy would strengthen our study. We had therefore added the following discussion to the revised manuscript:
“Enhancing the PPP in immune cells represents an emerging strategy to improve the efficacy of ICB in cancer therapy. Recent studies highlight its potential through improved T cell functionality and persistence in the TME. For instance, PPP activation has been shown to promote the generation and maintenance of TCF1 progenitor-like exhausted CD8 T cells, thereby enhancing tumor control when combined with PD-1 blockade. Another study demonstrates that the PPP metabolite Xu5P sustains the expansion of effector SLC35E2 CD8 progenitor-like exhausted T cells, and Xu5P supplementation synergizes with PD-1 blockade in tumor therapy. In our study, we found that PPP activation in DCs improved DC-mediated antitumor immunity. Moreover, PPP activation in DCs enhanced the therapeutic efficacy of anti-PD-L1 therapy. In conclusion, both previous reports and our current work suggest that activating the PPP in T cells or DCs constitutes a promising strategy for improving immunotherapy outcomes. Thus, selectively activating the PPP in T cells or DCs, in combination with ICB, represents a promising tumor therapy strategy worthy of investigation.”
In summary, the incorporation of above additional experiments and expanded discussion has strengthened the overall quality of our manuscript.
Minor Comments
1. Figure 2D, 2H, S2B, S2C, S2F, S2G, S8A-C: The data presentation is not appropriate. The authors normalized all values by dividing by 10³, which obscures the actual magnitude of differences. It would be more informative to present the raw MFI values directly and then assess the differences between groups accordingly. Please revise the figure and reanalyze the data.
Response: We thank for the reviewer’s helpful comments and for raising this point regarding the data presentation in our figures. Regarding your comments on Figures 2D, 2H, S2B, S2C, S2F, S2G, and S8A-C, we sincerely apologize for the confusion caused by our axis labeling. We would like to clarify that the raw MFI values were not normalized or divided by 10³. To make the axis labels more compact, we used the notation “10³” to represent thousands (e.g., labeling '1000' as '10³'). We realize now that this presentation was ambiguous and misleading, for which we take full responsibility.
To address these comments, we had revised all the mentioned figures in our revised manuscript. The axis labels had been updated to display the full, raw MFI values without the "10³" abbreviation. And we had confirmed that all statistical analyses and conclusions remain unchanged, as they were always based on the raw data. We sincerely appreciate your attention to detail, which has been instrumental in improving the clarity of our manuscript.
2. In Figure 4D, the actin loading control appears inconsistent across samples, which raises concerns about normalization. The authors should clarify or provide quantification to ensure reliability of the results.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s careful observation and helpful suggestion for our manuscript. To address the comments, we had now quantified the Western blot signals for p-STING, p-STAT1, p-AKT, and actin using ImageJ in Figure 4d. The results confirmed that PPP deficiency significantly suppressed STING signaling and downstream JAK-STAT activation, without notably affecting the PI3K-AKT pathway (Figure 4d). And we had incorporated the quantitative data, expressed as phosphorylation-to-actin ratios, into the revised manuscript to enhance clarity and strengthen the support for our conclusions.
3. In Figure 6B, DC numbers are presented without accounting for differences in tumor size. Normalization to tumor weight (e.g., DCs per gram tumor) would allow more accurate comparisons.
Response: We sincerely apologize for the lack of clarity in our original manuscript and thank the reviewer for highlighting this important point. We would like to clarify that the immune cell counts presented in Figure 6b, 6f, and 6j were already normalized per g of tumor tissue. To prevent any potential misunderstanding, we have revised the corresponding figure legends to explicitly state: "Flow cytometry analysis of the numbers of tumor-infiltrating CD11c , CD4 T, and CD8 T cells per g of tumor tissue." This revision ensures transparency in data normalization and enables accurate cross-group comparisons independent of tumor size variations.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
In the manuscript “Tumor immunoediting shapes pentose phosphate pathway to dictate DC function”, Liu et al. demonstrate that late-stage tumors exhibit reduced pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) activity, which correlates with a diminished ability to activate T cells within the tumor. Their findings suggest that the tumor microenvironment suppresses PPP activity, which is essential for fueling purine metabolism and providing ATP and GTP for 2’3’-cGAMP synthesis and cGAS activity. Reduced PPP activity ultimately leads to impaired cGAS signaling in dendritic cells and decreased expression of type I interferon genes.
The concept of the manuscript is well formulated, and the in vitro experiments using bone marrow–derived dendritic cells to show how PPP activity supports cGAS activation were interesting and well executed. However, the in vivo results that form the basis of the authors’ hypothesis and subsequent experiments lack critical controls and fail to account for the functional diversity of dendritic cells, which varies by origin (type 1 or type 2 DC) and maturation state (e.g., CCR7 DCs). Although the authors performed single-cell RNA sequencing of dendritic cells and highlighted their heterogeneity, all in vivo experiments were conducted on total dendritic cells. This is problematic because CCR7 mature dendritic cells are known to be the primary subset capable of activating T cells in tumors, and DC1 and DC2 populations differ in their ability to cross-present antigens.
Response: We thank the reviewer for their time and constructive comments on our manuscript. We fully acknowledge the importance of DC functional diversity. In response, we have performed additional experiments and analyses focusing on cDC1, cDC2, and CCR7 DC subsets to address the concerns raised. We believe these additions substantially strengthen the study. Below is our point-by-point response. Corresponding revisions in the manuscript text are highlighted in blue.
Below are specific comments to improve and strengthen the manuscript:
Major Points
1. Figure 1: The metabolomics assay is not described in the Materials and Methods section. How was it performed on tumor-infiltrating DCs? Without this information, it is difficult to interpret the results-specifically, the number and type of cells analyzed.
Response: We thank for the valuable comments. To address the reviewer’s question, we had added the detailed methods of metabolomics in the Materials and Methods section in the revised manuscript as follows: “Metabolite extraction and mass spectrometry-based metabolomics analysis: 2x106 late- and early-stage intratumoral cDCs (live CD45+CD24-F4/80-Ly6C-CD11c+MHC-II+) were isolated by flow cytometry from MC38 inoculated wild-type mice. Cell pellet was collected by centrifuging at 1000 rpm and 4 for 5 min. Samples were mixed with 500 µL extraction buffer (methanol: water = 3:1, containing 0.5×internal standard). After placement on dry ice for pre-cooling, the samples underwent three freeze-thaw cycles in liquid nitrogen, followed by vortex for 30 s to mix well. Subsequent sonication was performed in an ice-water bath for 15 min, and samples were then incubated at -40 °C for 1h. Following centrifugation at 12000 rpm and 4 °C for 15 min, 200 µL of supernatant was collected into a 2.0 mL tube and dried under vacuum. The dried residue was then reconstituted in 160 µL of methanol: acetonitrile: water (1:1:2, v/v/v). The solution was filtered and placed into an autosampler vial for liquid chromatography-high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC-MS). For reversed-phase (RP) system, an Agilent 1290 UPLC system equipped with an ACQUITY UPLC BEH C18 column (1.7 µm, 2.1 × 150 mm) was used. For hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography (HILIC) system, the same UPLC system was employed with an Atlantis Premier BEH Z-HILIC column (1.7 µm, 2.1 × 150 mm). An AB Sciex Triple Quad 6500+ mass spectrometer was used for metabolite detection. Raw LC–MS/MS data were processed using SCIEX Analyst Workstation Software (v1.7.3), and metabolite quantification was performed with the automated analysis software BIOTREE Bio Bud (v2.0.3)”.
2. How did the authors define the DC population in the single-cell dataset? Can they compare their data to publicly available dendritic cell signatures? How do they explain the absence of mature DCs in their single-cell analysis?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer's insightful comments and valuable suggestions.
For the identification of DC populations in the single-cell dataset, we referred to established DC-specific signatures and markers from previous published studies (Brown et al., 2019; Gerhard et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020). First, cell clusters expressing high levels of lineage markers (Cd3d, Cd19, Ncr1, Adgre1) were excluded. Subsequently, cDCs were defined based on canonical markers: Itgax, Flt3, and Zbtb46 (Figure III).
Figure III: The identification of DC populations in the single-cell dataset. (a and b) Dot plots show the expression levels of marker genes across different clusters. The expression levels of canonical marker genes used to exclude other cells (a), and the expression levels of DC lineage marker genes in each cluster from a (b).
The protocol was employed as follows and had been added in the Method section of the revised manuscript: “Cells displaying > 20% mitochondrial gene expression and > 5000 detected genes were filtered out. Clustering was done using the FindClusters() function with a resolution of 0.5. High lineage marker-expressing cell clusters (Cd3d, Cd19, Ncr1, Adgre1) were excluded. To investigate the potential function of cDCs, we further distinguished cDCs subpopulations (identified by Itgax, Flt3 and Zbtb46) from total DCs. Differential gene expression within specific clusters was explored with the FindMarkers() function, employing a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test by default.”
We apologize for the lack of clarity in our original manuscript, which led to the impression that mature DCs were absent. In fact, mature DCs are present in our dataset, as explicitly shown in the re-analyzed figures (Supplemental Figure 2, g and h). We fully agree with the reviewer's comments that CCR7 mature DCs (also known as mregDC) are known to be the primary subset capable of activating T cells in tumors, which were also proved by multitudinous previous studies (Lee et al., 2024; Maier et al., 2020; Ng et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019). Based on publicly established markers of mature DCs (identified by expression of Ccl22, Ccl17, and Ccr7) (Ng et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2020), we reanalyzed our single-cell RNA sequencing data to delineate this mature DC subpopulation. Our results further indicated that these existed a significant mature DC subpopulation both in early- and late-stage intratumoral DCs (Supplemental Figure 2, g and h), and the population of mature DCs from late tumors were downregulated compared to that in early tumors (Supplemental Figure 2i).
3. If different DC subsets were identified in the single-cell data, why were subsequent analyses performed on total DCs? Why were maturation markers and cytokines assessed in immature DCs rather than focusing on mature CCR7 DCs?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer's insightful comments, which led to a valuable improvement of our study.
We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this important point regarding the limitation of focusing solely on the total cDC population in our study. Our initial analyses on bulk cDCs, while identifying a global functional decline, lacked the resolution to attribute defects to specific functional subsets. In direct response to this comment, we have now performed a comprehensive re-analysis of our scRNA-seq data and conducted new experiments specifically on the sorted mature DC subset. As supported by latest studies, cDCs in the tumor microenvironment (TME) can be classified into three main subsets: cDC1, cDC2, and mature DCs (also referred to as mregDCs) (Lee et al., 2024; Maier et al., 2020; Ng et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2019). Among these, mature DCs represent the dominant subset responsible for mediating antitumor immunity and are thought to originate from cDC1 and cDC2 following tumor antigen uptake (Maier et al., 2020; Ng et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2019). Further analysis of our scRNA-seq data revealed a notable subset of mature DCs (defined by expression of Ccl22, Ccl17, and Ccr7) in late-stage tumors (Supplemental Figure 2, g and h). Flow cytometry analysis indicated the proportion of mature DCs was decreased in late-stage tumors (Supplemental Figure 2i). KEGG analysis confirmed that mature DCs from late-stage tumors displayed impaired antigen presentation capacity (Supplemental Figure 2k). Furthermore, we isolated mature DCs from early- and late-stage tumors and observed decreased expression of maturation markers and functional cytokines in the late-stage mature DCs (Supplemental Figure 2, l and m). Moreover, we isolated equal numbers of early- and late-stage mature DCs and co-cultured them with OT-I T cells in the presence of SIINFEKL peptide. Late-stage intratumoral mature DC demonstrated significantly reduced capacity to stimulate OT-I T cell proliferation (Figure 1, l and m) and effector cytokine production (Figure 1n) compared to their early-stage counterparts. In summary, these findings indicate that mature DCs in late-stage tumors exhibit functional impairment compared to those in early-stage tumors, which is consistent with our total cDCs phenotype.
These new findings do not contradict our initial observations on bulk cDCs; rather, they identify the mature DC subset as an important contributor to the overall functional impairment in our study. We believe this revision significantly strengthens the precision and impact of our study.
4. Figure 1: Why did the authors validate the single-cell data using qPCR? Can they validate CCR7 expression at the protein level? Does the downregulation of maturation genes indicate fewer mature DCs in the tumor or reduced protein levels within mature DCs?
Response: Thanks for the reviewer’s valuable comments. In response to the reviewer’s question, we assessed CCR7 protein expression by flow cytometry in early- and late-stage tumors. The results showed that CCR7 protein levels were lower in late-stage tumors (Supplemental Figure 2i). Further analysis revealed a notable reduction in the numbers of CCR7 DCs per g of tumor tissue in late-stage tumors (Supplemental Figure 2j). Together, these findings indicate that both CCR7 expression and the abundance of CCR7 DCs are diminished in late-stage tumors.
5. The GSEA was performed on total DCs. Could the authors identify mature DCs in the single-cell dataset and perform GSEA specifically on this population, which is responsible for T-cell activation?
Response: Thanks for the reviewer’s helpful suggestions. In response to the reviewer's comments, we reanalyzed our single-cell RNA sequencing data using established markers for mature DC subset (defined by expression of Ccl22, Ccl17, and Ccr7) (Maier et al., 2020; Ng et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2019), enabling clear identification of this subset within the total DC population (Supplemental Figure 2, g and h). Subsequent GSEA analysis revealed impaired antigen processing and presentation capacity in late-stage intratumoral mature DCs (Supplemental Figure 2k), a finding consistent with the functional defects observed in the total cDCs population.
6. For KEGG pathway analysis, it would be important to determine whether mature DCs exhibit lower PPP activity.
Response: We thank the reviewer for their valuable comments. To address the question, we performed KEGG pathway analysis. The analysis identified the PPP as one of the most significantly altered pathways in late-stage compared to early-stage mature DCs (Supplemental Figure 3d). We then isolated early- and late-stage intratumoral mature DCs and observed reduced levels of the key PPP metabolite NADPH in late-stage mature DCs (Supplemental Figure 3e). Additionally, qPCR analysis showed decreased mRNA expression of major PPP enzymes in late-stage mature DCs (Supplemental Figure 3f). Together, these findings demonstrate that late-stage intratumoral mature DCs exhibit impaired PPP activity.
7. Figure 2: The authors treated tumors with PPP inhibitors and assessed maturation markers. Instead, could they quantify the proportion of mature CCR7 DCs and measure the gMFI of maturation markers in this subset?
Response: We greatly appreciate the valuable suggestions provided by the reviewer and have performed additional experiments to address this concern. We isolated early-stage intratumoral DCs from MC38 tumor-bearing wild-type mice and treated them with the PPP inhibitor G6PDi-1 for 12 in vitro. Flow cytometric analysis revealed that PPP inhibition reduced the proportion of mature CCR7 DCs (Supplemental Figure 3g), consistent with our single-cell RNA sequencing data. Furthermore, PPP downregulation decreased expression of key maturation markers including MHC-I, CD80, and CD86 within the mature DC subset (Supplemental Figure 3h). These results demonstrate that PPP activity is essential for maintaining both the abundance and functional maturation of CCR7 DCs in the TME.
8. Figure 2: The description of how tumor DCs were recovered, stimulated, and re-injected is unclear. Were these total DCs? Were mature DCs excluded? Were DC1 and DC2 subsets considered? What was the viability of these cells after sorting and 12-hour in vitro stimulation prior to re-injection? Did the treatment induce maturation of immature DCs in vitro? How were injected and non-injected tumor DCs distinguished for comparison? The experimental design is not well explained. Were control samples injected with untreated tumor DCs recovered and re-injected after 12 hours? Did the treatment itself alter maturation markers before injection?
Response: We thank the reviewer for these detailed and critical questions, which have helped us notably improve the clarity of our experimental design.
For the DC population used, subset consideration, and exclusion: The transferred cells were total intratumoral cDCs, defined as live CD45 CD24- F4/80 Ly6C CD11c MHC-II cells. No subsets (including mature DCs, cDC1, or cDC2) were excluded. This population naturally contains a mixture of these subsets (Supplemental Figure 1). We chose this approach to model the therapeutic transfer of a total tumor-derived DC population. Furthermore, we had added detailed experimental design protocols of our DC-based therapy tumor model in the Method section of our revised manuscript “For another DC-based therapy tumor model, MC38 (5x105 cells per mouse) tumor-bearing wild-type mice (on day 6 post tumor cell inoculation) were subcutaneously injected adjacent to the tumors with 3x106 intratumoral cDCs. Early- and late-stage intratumoral cDCs were isolated from wild-type MC38 tumor-bearing mice (5×10⁵ cells per mouse) at day 10 and day 20 post-inoculation, respectively. Intratumoral cDCs (live CD45+CD24-F4/80-Ly6C-CD11c+MHC-II+) were isolated by flow cytometry. Early-stage intratumoral cDCs were treated with PPP inhibitors (G6PDi-1 or 6-AN) or untreated (Ctrl) for 12h in vitro, and late-stage intratumoral cDCs were treated with the PPP agonist AG1 or untreated (Ctrl) for 12h in vitro prior to subcutaneous injection.”
For the cell viability post-sorting and treatment: After sorting and the 12h in vitro treatment with PPP modulators (G6PDi-1, 6-AN, AG1) or control, cell viability was uncompromised (Supplemental Figure 3, k and l).
For the effect of in vitro treatment on DC maturation: The results demonstrated that the 12h treatment itself directly altered the maturation state of DCs prior to injection. PPP inhibition via G6PDi-1 or 6-AN downregulated DC maturation markers and functional gene expression (Figure 2, d-f), whereas PPP activation via AG1 enhanced these parameters (Figure 2, j-l).
For the distinguishing injected compared to non-injected DCs: In this model, different groups of mice received DCs subjected to different in vitro treatments. The comparison is made between these independent experimental groups.
For the control group: The critical control group consisted of mice injected with DCs that underwent the identical process of sorting and 12h in vitro culture but in the absence of PPP modulators (the “untreated Ctrl” group in our description).
We have incorporated all these details into the revised Methods section and Figure legends. This incorporation has notably helped improve the quality of our manuscript.
9. Still in Figure 2: When augmenting PPP activity, the authors assessed maturation markers by qPCR in total DCs. Could they instead quantify mature DCs in the tumor and measure gMFI of maturation and activation markers? It is difficult to conclude that PPP activity impacts DC maturation and activation based solely on RNA levels in total DCs.
Response: We are deeply grateful for the reviewer's insightful suggestions. In response to this valuable feedback, we have conducted additional experiments to address this important concern. Late-stage tumor-infiltrating cDCs were isolated from MC38 tumor-bearing mice and treated in vitro with the PPP agonist AG1 or untreated for 12h. Flow cytometry analysis revealed that PPP activation increased the proportion of mature DCs (Supplemental Figure 3i). Further analysis on mature DCs showed elevated expression of maturation and activation markers including MHC-I, CD80, and CD86 following AG1 treatment (Supplemental Figure 3j). These results collectively demonstrate that PPP activation promotes the maturation and activation of intratumoral mature DCs.
10. Figure 3: Could the authors quantify mature DCs in tumors from G6pdx / ⁺⁺ Zbtb46-Cre (WT) and KO mice? Also, assess immature DC1 and DC2 infiltration to determine whether KO DCs have reduced tumor infiltration capacity.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's valuable comments. To address the questions raised, we inoculated G6pdx / Zbtb46-Cre (WT) and ⁺⁺ G6pdxfl/flZbtb46-Cre (KO) mice with MC38 tumor cells. Our results indicated that the proportions of CCR7 DCs (mature DCs) and cDC1s were decreased in KO mice compared to WT mice, whereas the percentage of cDC2s remained unchanged (Supplemental Figure 5b). Furthermore, the absolute numbers of CCR7 DCs, cDC1s and cDC2s per g of tumor tissue were all reduced in KO mice (Supplemental Figure 5c). These findings demonstrate that PPP deficiency in cDCs impairs the tumor infiltration capacity of mature and cDC1 subsets.
11. Figure 4: The rationale for injecting G6pdx / Zbtb46-Cre (WT) and KO BMDCs into tumors and monitoring tumor growth is unclear. If the TME impairs ⁺⁺ PPP activity in DCs, why would WT BMDCs be unaffected? Wouldn’t WT BMDCs also experience PPP suppression? Please clarify.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comments, which raise an important theoretical consideration regarding the suppressive nature of the TME. We agree that if the TME broadly impairs PPP activity in all infiltrating DCs, the functional difference between wild-type (WT) and PPP-deficient (KO) cells might be attenuated.
The primary objective of our adoptive DC transfer model is precisely to isolate and evaluate the cell-intrinsic functional consequence of PPP deficiency, independent of the complex systemic metabolic suppression imposed by the established TME. To achieve this, we pulsed and activated BMDCs with a defined antigen (SIINFEKL peptide) and a potent stimulant (ISD) in vitro before transfer. This critical step generates a cohort of DCs that have initiated their antigen-presentation and maturation programs under controlled, optimal conditions prior to encountering the TME. Our in vitro data already established that PPP deficiency intrinsically impairs DC antigen-presenting capacity (Figure 3, b-d).
In this experimental framework, the transferred WT BMDCs serve as a baseline for “the maximal antitumor function achievable by DCs upon proper in vitro activation.” Upon peritumoral injection, both WT and KO DCs are subjected to the same immunosuppressive TME. The key question our experiment addresses is: Does an intrinsic, genetic deficiency in the PPP impair the ability of KO DCs to sustain this pre-activated functional state and effectively prime tumor-specific CD8 T cells in vivo, compared to PPP competent (WT) DCs? Our in vivo data provide a clear answer: Despite identical in vitro activation and facing the same TME, KO DCs exhibited a significantly reduced capacity to control tumor growth compared to the WT DC group (Figure 4, f and g, and Supplemental Figure 5, i-l). These results demonstrate that PPP is an indispensable, cell-intrinsic determinant of DC function. Therefore, our model does not assume that WT DCs are unaffected by the TME. Instead, it reveals that intrinsic PPP activity is a critical metabolic node governing DC efficacy, and its loss undermines DC function.
12. What is ISD, which was used to stimulate BMDCs?
Response: We apologize for any confusion. Interferon-stimulatory DNA (ISD) is a well-established agonist of the cGAS-STING signaling pathway. It can be recognized by cGAS, leading to this pathway activation, and has been widely utilized across numerous studies to stimulate cGAS-STING signaling (Cho et al., 2024; Fang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Mukai et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2025). Furthermore, we have now included a detailed description of the ISD sequence and its synthesis method in the Methods section of the revised manuscript: “The ISD used in this study was prepared with equimolar amounts of oligonucleotides: F: 5′-TACAGATCTACTAGTGATCTATGACTGATCTGTACATGATCTACATACAGATCTACTAGTGATCTATGACTGATCTGTACATGATCTACA-3′; R: 5′-TGTAGATCATGTACAGATCAGTCATAGATCACTAGTAGATCTGTATGTAGATCATGTACAGATCAGTCATAGATCACTAGTAGATCTGTA-3′. The oligonucleotides were annealed in PBS at 70 for 30 minutes before cooling to room temperature.” Additionally, we have also added the following description of ISD in the Results section of the revised manuscript:
“Furthermore, we cultured WT and KO BMDCs in vitro and stimulated them with the STING signaling agonist Interferon Stimulatory DNA (ISD, a synthetic double-stranded DNA that sensed by cGAS to activate the cGAS-STING pathway). Our results indeed confirmed that PPP deficiency impaired STING signaling (Supplemental Figure 6, a and b).”
13. Figure 4J: The rationale for comparing tumor growth after injection of WT versus STING-pathway KO BMDCs is unclear. How do the authors explain that injected BMDCs promote tumor growth compared to WT BMDCs? Please comment.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this comment and apologize for any lack of clarity.
First, Figure 4f (former manuscript Figure 4j) is a DC adoptive transfer model to evaluate DC function. In this model, BMDCs were pulsed with SIINFEKL peptide and transferred into MC38-OVA tumor-bearing wild-type mice. Impaired function of the transferred DCs would be expected to result in accelerated tumor growth. As shown in Figure 4f, mice receiving STING-KO DCs exhibited faster tumor growth compared to those receiving wild-type DCs, suggesting that STING deficiency impairs DC function. While this phenotype is also supported by our previous work (Hu et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2023), we acknowledge that the direct evidence linking STING deficiency in DCs to their functional impairment was not explicitly provided in the manuscript, which likely caused confusion. To address this directly, we added an in vitro assay. WT and STING-KO BMDCs were pulsed with SIINFEKL peptide and co-cultured separately with OT-I T cells. Compared to WT BMDCs, STING-KO BMDCs showed a significantly reduced capacity to stimulate OT-I T cell proliferation and effector cytokine production. These results confirm STING deficiency intrinsically impairs DC function (Figure IV).
Figure IV: STING deficiency intrinsically impairs DC function. 1x105 OT-I T cells were cultured with 3x104 wild-type (WT) and Tmem173-/- (STING deficient) BMDCs in the presence of SIINFEKL peptides (n = 5). (a) Flow cytometry analysis (left) and graph presentation (right) of CFSE. (b and c) Flow cytometry analysis of Ki-67+ (b), IFN-+, TNF-+ and GZMB+ (c) T cells. Data were presented as mean ± SEM. Data were analyzed through two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-tests. n indicates the number of biological replicates.
Second, the purpose of Figure 4f was not to prove that STING is critical for DC function-a well-established concept in the literature-but rather to determine whether the antitumor function impairment caused by PPP deficiency is STING-dependent. To this end, we transferred WT, PPP-KO, STING-KO, and double-knockout (DKO; PPP-KO & STING-KO) DCs into MC38-OVA tumor-bearing mice. As expected, PPP-KO DCs accelerated tumor growth compared to WT DCs. Crucially, tumor growth in mice receiving STING-KO DCs was not further accelerated by the additional loss of PPP (DKO vs STING-KO). This indicates that PPP deficiency does not exacerbate the functional impairment observed upon STING deletion, demonstrating that PPP mediates DC antitumor function in a STING-dependent manner.
14. Figure 6: Does treatment with ATP and GTP induce maturation in KO DCs? Is the observed effect due to injecting mature BMDCs? Why is there no effect in WT BMDCs treated with ATP and GTP? The lack of tumor growth reduction in WT suggests that supplementation is insufficient to overcome PPP deficiency. How do the authors explain that KO BMDCs promote tumor growth and that supplementation restores tumor growth to WT levels?
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for their valuable comments and apologize for any confusion.
In Figure 6a, the concentration of ATP and GTP (100 µM) was selected based on our experimental data. This dose of ATP and GTP was sufficient to restore the function of PPP deficient (KO) DCs without affecting wild-type (WT) DCs. We acknowledge that these supporting data were not included in the original manuscript, which led to the misunderstanding. Therefore, we have now added them in the revised manuscript.
Specifically, WT and KO BMDCs were cultured and treated with different concentrations of ATP and GTP for 12h in vitro. First, we confirmed that PPP deficiency reduced the expression of maturation markers including MHC-I, CD80, and CD86 in DCs (Supplemental Figure 8, e and f). Supplementation with 100 µM ATP and GTP restored the expression of these maturation markers in KO DCs to levels comparable to WT DCs, without altering expression in WT DCs (Supplemental Figure 8, e and f). Higher concentrations (300 and 500 µM) enhanced maturation in both WT and KO DCs (Supplemental Figure 8, e and f). To ensure the rationality of our experiments, 100 µM was selected as the working concentration for subsequent studies. Correspondingly, qPCR analysis confirmed that 100 µM ATP and GTP supplementation also rescued the expression of functional cytokines in KO DCs without affecting WT DCs (Supplemental Figure 8g). Therefore, in Figure 6a, we observed that supplementing WT DCs with 100 µM ATP and GTP did not affect tumor growth compared to untreated WT DCs. More importantly, supplementing KO DCs with ATP and GTP significantly delayed tumor growth compared to untreated KO DCs, restoring it to the level observed with WT DCs.
In summary, our results demonstrate that PPP deficiency in DCs impairs purine metabolism, leading to reduced ATP and GTP levels. Supplementation with ATP and GTP rescues the maturation, functional cytokine expression, and antitumor immunity of PPP-deficient DCs.
15. Do KO BMDCs become more immunosuppressive in the tumor compared to WT BMDCs?
Response: We thank the reviewer for their helpful suggestion and have performed additional experiments to address this point. We cultured WT and PPP deficient BMDCs, and then labeled them with CFSE (carboxyfluorescein succinimidyl ester) in vitro. The labeled BMDCs were then injected subcutaneously adjacent to established tumors. After 24h, we checked the PD-L1 expression on CFSE-labelled DCs. Our results indicated that KO DCs displayed higher expression level of PD-L1, indicating an acquisition of an immunosuppressive molecular profile. Furthermore, we isolated CFSE-labeled WT and KO BMDCs from the tumors in equal numbers and co-cultured them separately with OT-I T cells in the presence of the SIINFEKL peptide. Compared to WT BMDCs, the KO BMDCs exhibited a significantly reduced capacity to stimulate OT-I T cell proliferation and effector cytokine production (Figure V).
In summary, our results demonstrate KO BMDCs become more immunosuppressive in the tumor compared to WT BMDCs.
Figure V: PPP deficient DCs acquire a suppressive phenotype in the tumors. (a) Flow cytometry analysis of CFSE+ BMDCs. (b) Flow cytometry analysis (left) and graph presentation (right) of expression of PD-L1 on DC (n = 5). (c) Flow cytometry analysis (left) and graph presentation (right) of CFSE+ T cells. (d-e) Flow cytometry analysis of Ki-67+ (d, n = 5), IFN-+, TNF-+ and GZMB+ (e,n = 5) T cells. Data were presented as mean ± SEM. Data were analyzed through two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-tests. In b-e, n indicates the number of biological replicates.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Several studies in pre-clinical models have demonstrated an indispensable role for conventional dendritic cells (cDCs), particularly cDC1s, in promoting T cell responses to cancer and augmenting the efficacy of T cell based immunotherapies. While the link between cancer immunity and cDCs has been extensively studied, there is now growing interest in understanding the cell intrinsic determinants of cDC that govern cDC function.
Work from Liu et al. reports cDC metabolism as a key component of their anti-tumour activity. The authors showed that the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) is essential for cDC activation and their capacity to prime T cells. Although PPP activity is evident in intratumoural cDCs at early stages, it becomes suppressed during later stages of tumour progression, thereby contributing to immune evasion. Using conditional knockout mouse models and ex vivo/in vitro assays, the authors further showed that PPP deficiency compromises STING phosphorylation and downstream signaling. Pharmacological activation of the PPP restores antitumor immunity and enhances the efficacy of immune checkpoint blocakde. Finally, analysis of human breast cancer samples reveals that the expression of key PPP enzymes correlates with signatures of intratumoral cDC accumulation. While the mechanism proposed by the authors meets the novelty criteria expected for publication in Nature Communications and the experiments are generally well designed, the following points need to be addressed to improve the clarity and overall quality of the manuscript.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for their careful consideration of our manuscript and for providing these valuable comments, which have helped to improve our study. Please see below our point-by-point response to each comment, including revisions to the manuscript. Major revisions to the manuscript text have been highlighted in blue.
Major points:
1. It would be important to clarify whether the cDC1 or cDC2 ratio is maintained between early- and late-stage tumours. If this is not the case, it becomes difficult to draw firm conclusions from the T cell activation assays, as the observed differences in ex vivo T cell priming could result either from functional impairment of cDC subsets or from numerical differences in cDC1 and cDC2 populations between early and late tumours. The authors should therefore normalize the T cell activation assays based on the cDC1 and cDC2 ratio to ensure comparability between the groups.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. To address these comments, we performed the following additional experiments.
First, we quantified cDC1 and cDC2 proportions in early- and late-stage tumors by flow cytometry. The proportion of cDC1 was significantly lower in late-stage than in early-stage tumors, whereas the proportion of cDC2 was comparable between the two stages (Supplemental Figure 2i).
Second, to assess the functional capacity of these subsets, we isolated equal numbers of cDC1 from early- and late-stage tumors and co-cultured them separately with OT-I T cells in the presence of SIINFEKL peptide. Late-stage cDC1 showed markedly reduced ability to stimulate OT-I T cell proliferation (Figure 1, o and p) and effector cytokine production (Figure 1q) compared to early-stage cDC1. Furthermore, we performed similar experiments with cDC2 using OT-II T cells and observed a similar functional decline. Late-stage cDC2 were significantly less capable of promoting OT-II T cell proliferation and cytokine production than early-stage cDC2 (Figure 1, r-t).
Together, these results demonstrate that even when controlling for subset frequency by using equal cell numbers, both cDC1 and cDC2 in late-stage tumors exhibit intrinsic functional impairment. This confirms that the diminished T cell priming capacity observed in bulk assays is due to cell-autonomous dysfunction, not merely changes in DC subset composition.
2. In Figure 1, it would be important to determine whether the activation of both cDC subsets (cDC1 and cDC2) as well as their ability to prime T cells are equally affected by the suppression of PPP-pathway in late tumours. Identifying which subset is primarily impacted would enhance the mechanistic understanding of this study. To this end, the authors should repeat the T cell activation assays using separately purified cDC1 and cDC2 populations.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s valuable suggestion. To address these comments, we isolated equal numbers of cDC1 or cDC2 from early- and late-stage tumors, respectively. We then co-cultured cDC1 with OT-I T cells, and cDC2 with OT-II T cells in the presence of SIINFEKL peptide. Our results showed that late-stage intratumoral cDC1 exhibited a markedly reduced capacity to stimulate OT-I T cell proliferation (Figure 1, o and p) and effector cytokine production (Figure 1q) compared to early-stage cDC1. Similarly, late-stage cDC2 were significantly less effective at promoting OT-II T cell proliferation and cytokine production than early-stage cDC2 (Figure 1, r-t).
Together, these findings demonstrate that both cDC1 and cDC2 from late-stage tumors exhibit substantially impaired T cell priming capacity. Importantly, the degree of functional impairment was comparable between the two subsets. This indicates that the suppression of the PPP in the late tumor microenvironment does not preferentially affect one conventional DC subset over another; rather, it broadly compromises the functional fitness of the entire intratumoral cDC compartment.
3. In Figures 3E and F, the appropriate control for G6pdxfl/flZbtb46-Cre mice is G6pdxfl/fl; the authors should repeat the tumour growth profile using this control line for accurate comparison. Alternatively, the authors could provide tumour growth data of WT, Zbtb46-Cre and G6pdxfl/fl within the same experiment to demonstrate that tumour progression is comparable across these lines and that they can be used interchangeably.
Response: We greatly appreciate the valuable suggestions provided by the reviewer, and have performed additional experiments to address this concern.
We subcutaneously inoculated G6pdxfl/fl and G6pdxfl/flZbtb46-Cre mice with MC38 tumor cells. Consistent with our observations in Figure 3e, the results confirmed G6PDX deficiency in cDCs accelerates tumor growth (Figure VI).
Figure VI: G6PDXdeficiency in cDCs accelerates tumor growth. Tumor growth of G6pdxfl/fland G6pdxfl/flZbtb46-Cremice (n = 9). Data were presented as mean ± SEM and were analyzed through two-way ANOVA analyses. n indicates the number of mice.
4. Given that PPP-deficient cDCs show impaired ability to prime antigen-specific T cells, it would be important to clarify whether the tumour growth retardation observed in mice with enhanced cDC PPP activity is CD8 T cell-dependent. The authors could address this by depleting CD8 T cells using specific antibodies in mice adoptively transferred with cDCs exhibiting enhanced PPP activity.
Response:We thank the reviewer for this important suggestion. To directly test whether the antitumor effect of enhanced PPP activity in cDCs depends on CD8 T cells, we performed an in vivo depletion experiment. Wild-type mice receiving adoptive transfer of AG1-augmented cDCs were treated with anti-CD8 depleting antibody. Flow cytometry confirmed efficient depletion of CD8 T cells in vivo. Compared to untreated DCs, AG1-augmented DCs significantly inhibited tumor growth. As anticipated, CD8 T cell depletion completely abrogated the tumor growth inhibition mediated by AG1-treated DCs. Furthermore, CD8 T cell depletion eliminating the therapeutic difference between AG1-treated and untreated DC groups (Figure VII). Together, these results demonstrate that the antitumor effect mediated by enhanced PPP activity in cDCs is strictly CD8 T cell-dependent.
Figure VII: The antitumor effect mediated by enhanced PPP activity in cDCs is strictly CD8 T cell-dependent. Wild-type mice were inoculated with MC38-OVA tumor cells. Anti-CD8 (200 μg per mouse) or isotype control IgG was administered intraperitoneally one day prior to tumor challenge and then every three days for a total of four doses. BMDCs were pulsed with SIINFEKL peptide for 12h, incubated with AG1 (3 µM) or untreated (Ctrl) for 4h, and subsequently injected subcutaneously adjacent to established tumors on days 3 and 6 post-tumor inoculation. a: Flow cytometry analysis of CD8. b: Tumor growth of wild-type mice (n = 9). Data were presented as mean ± SEM. (b) was analyzed through two-way ANOVA analyses with Tukey’s multiple comparison test.In b, n indicates the number of mice.
Minor but essential points:
1. Figure legends should be revised for clarity and completeness, explicitly stating the number and type of replicates in each panel (e.g., whether each point in the graphs represents a biological or technical replicate).
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this important suggestion. We have thoroughly revised the legends for all figures in the revised manuscript to ensure clarity and completeness.
2. The statement on lines 152-153 “Consistent with the metabolic profiling, late-stage intratumoral cDCs exhibited markedly decreased NADPH and R5P production (Figure 2B)." is not adequately supported by data and should be revised or removed.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's comprehensive evaluation of our manuscript and so sorry for the mistake. To address the reviewer’s suggestion, we had included statistical analysis of the metabolic profiling data in Supplemental Figure 3a. The results confirmed that levels of key PPP metabolites were significantly reduced in late-stage intratumoral cDCs. Accordingly, we had revised the corresponding statement in the revised manuscript to: "Consistent with the metabolic profiling, late-stage intratumoral cDCs exhibited markedly decreased NADPH and R5P production (Supplemental Figure 3a)."
3. The authors should clearly define every gene, abbreviation, and mouse model used in the figures and main text. For example, specify which protein is absent in TmemKO mice. Figure legends should be self-explanatory and allow readers to interpret the data without referring to the methods section. Similarly, in figure 5 and 6, please clarify in the panels the exact genotypes of the WT and KO mice.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this critical point regarding manuscript clarity. We have thoroughly revised the manuscript to address this as follows:
For the Definitions and abbreviations: All non-standard gene symbols, protein names, and abbreviations have been clearly defined upon first use in both the main text and the figure legends.
For the mouse model clarification: The specific genetic alteration for each knockout mouse model is now explicitly stated in the Methods section and reiterated in the relevant figure legends. For example, we have specified that "Tmem173-/-" refers to mice with a knockout of the STING gene.
For the Figure legends: All figure legends have been revised in revised manuscript. We have stated the exact genotypes of the mice used in each experiment directly in the legends for Figures 5 and 6.
These comprehensive edits ensure that readers can accurately interpret all data presented without needing to cross-reference the Methods section, significantly improving the quality of our manuscript.
4. The combination “A + G + ISD” requires clarification. The authors should specify in both the main text and figure legend what each acronym represents and briefly describes the mechanism of action (text and methods) of these STING agonists, particularly in contrast to the other cGAS/STING agonists used elsewhere in the manuscript.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for highlighting this lack of clarity.
First, we have specified in both the main text and figure legends what each acronym represents. For example, we have clarified the "A+G+ISD" combination throughout the manuscript, now explicitly defining it as "ATP+ GTP+ISD" in the relevant text and Figure legends.
Second, we have briefly described the mechanism of action of these STING agonists used in our study and added in our revised manuscript: ISD (a synthetic double-stranded DNA that sensed by cGAS to activates the cGAS-STING pathway); DMXAA (a direct small-molecule binder of murine STING); cGAMP (the natural enzymatic product of cGAS that directly binds and activates STING).
5. It would be interesting to investigate whether a high PPP-related gene signature enhances the predictive value of the cDC1 gene signature (e.g. comparing patients with high PPP/high cDC1, low PPP/high cDC1, low PPP/low cDC1, high PPP/low cDC1 expression). The authors could analysis some of the TCGA datasets previously used to show that intratumoral cDC1 gene signatures positively correlate with patient survival, as reported by JP Böttcher et al., 2018 (DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2018.01.004 )
Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable comments. In response to the reviewer's suggestion (Böttcher et al., 2018), we first analyzed the correlation between cDC1- and PPP-related gene signatures using TCGA datasets. The results revealed a positive correlation between these signatures in breast cancer (BRCA) (Figure 7a). We next examined whether incorporating the PPP gene signature could improve the prognostic value of the cDC signature alone. Analysis showed that patients classified as cDChiPPPhi had the most favorable overall survival, while those in the cDClowPPPlow group exhibited the poorest outcomes in BRCA (Supplemental Figure 10b). Collectively, these findings position the PPP as a key metabolic determinant of cDC-mediated antitumor immunity, with combined cDC and PPP signatures offering enhanced prognostic stratification in BRCA.
6. The title should be changed and refined based on the data the authors have provided. There is no experimental evidence for tumour immunoediting- immunoediting refers historically to the experiments that have been conducted by R D Schreiber’s group, none of which are listed in this manuscript.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s comprehensive consideration of our manuscript. We agree that our study does not provide direct experimental evidence for the broader process of tumor immunoediting. Our work instead focuses on how alterations in the PPP within intratumoral cDCs impact their antitumor functionality. In response to the reviewer's suggestion, we have revised the manuscript title to: "Pentose phosphate pathway fuels cGAS-STING signaling to boost intratumoral cDC function." We believe this title more accurately reflects the central findings and scope of our study.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
In the current study, Ben Liu et al. demonstrate that defects in the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) occur in late-stage tumor-infiltrated dendritic cells (DCs). Impairment of the PPP reduces the levels of purine nucleotides ATP and GTP, which are essential substrates for cGAS enzymatic activity. This, in turn, results in insufficient activation of the STING pathway and consequently dampens DC function, limiting their antigen presentation capacity and cytokine production. The study identifies a critical role for the PPP in dysfunctional tumor-derived DCs and highlights a positive feedback loop between the PPP and STING pathways, providing potential therapeutic targets and mechanistic insights for enhancing DC function in cancer therapy.
The following are our comments and suggestions that the authors may consider to further strengthen their study:
Response: We sincerely thank reviewer for their time and effort in reviewing our manuscript. We are particularly grateful for the insightful comments and constructive suggestions aimed at strengthening our study. We have carefully considered all points raised and have performed additional experiments. Below is our point-by-point response. Corresponding revisions in the manuscript text are highlighted in blue.
1. Can the authors examine the levels of pyrimidines in early- versus late-stage tumor-derived DCs?
Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestions. To address this question, we measured pyrimidine levels in early- and late-stage tumor-infiltrating cDCs using mass spectrometry. The results showed decreased levels of cytosine and uracil in late-stage intratumoral cDCs (Figure VIII). We also assessed ribose 5-phosphate (R5P), a precursor metabolite for pyrimidine synthesis in the PPP. R5P levels were significantly lower in late-stage cDCs compared to early-stage cells (Supplemental Figure 3a). Moreover, supplementation with R5P restored STING signaling in G6PDX-deficient DCs (Supplemental Figure 7, g and h). In summary, these findings indicate that impaired PPP activity in late-stage intratumoral cDCs leads to reduced accumulation of pyrimidines.
Figure VIII: PPP activity in late-stage intratumoral cDCs leads to reduced accumulation of pyrimidines. Graph presentation of cytosine (a) and uracil (b) in late-stage intratumoral cDCs (n = 4). Data were presented as mean ± SEM. Data were analyzed through two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-tests. In a and b, n indicates the number of mice.
2. The authors report that ROS accumulation is a consequence of PPP deficiency in DCs. Could they provide data on both mitochondrial and cellular ROS levels in early- and late-stage DCs?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer's insightful comments. Our study demonstrated that impaired PPP activity in late-stage tumor-infiltrating cDCs compromised their functionality. As PPP supplies NADPH and R5P (Supplemental Figure 7a). NADPH actively contributes to maintaining redox homeostasis. Our data also showed that PPP deficiency in DCs led to heightened ROS accumulation in vitro (Supplemental Figure 7d). In response to the reviewer's suggestion, we further assessed whether ROS accumulation also occurs in late-stage intratumoral cDCs in vivo. Measurement of both cellular and mitochondrial ROS revealed significantly higher levels in late-stage intratumoral cDCs compared to early-stage counterparts (Supplemental Figure 7, b and c). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that PPP impairment in late-stage intratumoral cDCs induces ROS accumulation.
3. Since purine levels are reduced in late-stage DCs, does this lead to DNA damage in these cells?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s helpful comments and have included additional experiments. To address the question, we isolated early- and late-stage tumor-infiltrating cDCs from MC38 tumor-bearing wild-type mice. As a positive control for DNA damage induction, BMDCs were treated with 100 μM etoposide. Western blot analysis of γH2AX-a well-established marker of DNA damage-revealed no significant difference between early- and late-stage intratumoral cDCs (Supplemental Figure 7p). To further validate this observation, we compared wild-type and G6PDX deficient BMDCs and similarly observed no increase in DNA damage upon PPP disruption (Supplemental Figure 7o). In summary, our data indicate PPP deficiency and the associated purine depletion in DCs do not lead to elevated DNA damage.
4. Could the authors elaborate on why PPP deficiency induces PD-L1 expression in DCs? Given that STING activation has previously been shown to promote PD-L1 expression and support DC activation, how do these findings align?
Response: We are deeply grateful for the reviewer's insightful comments. This is an excellent and critical point which is deserved to be discussed in the manuscript.
To address the comments, we have included detailed discussion in the DISCUSSION section in our revised manuscript as follow: “PD-L1 expression on DCs is critical for their survival, functionality, and response to ICB (Oh et al., 2020; Peng et al., 2020; Xiao et al., 2024). Our findings indicated that PPP deficiency upregulates PD-L1 expression in intratumoral cDCs. This observation appears to contrast with a recent report demonstrating that STING activation robustly increases PD-L1 expression in monocytes via the STING-IRF3-type I interferon axis(Song et al., 2025). Such a discrepancy suggests that the relationship between STING signaling and PD-L1 expression may be cell-type-specific. PPP deficiency impairs NADPH production, leading to ROS accumulation. Elevated ROS levels are known to activate signaling pathways that induce PD-L1 expression in non-small cell lung cancer (Liu et al., 2023). We observed that PPP deficiency in cDCs induced ROS accumulation, which may contribute to increased PD-L1 levels. While our study establishes a link between PPP deficiency and PD-L1 upregulation in intratumoral cDCs, the precise molecular mechanisms warrant further investigation.”
5. Metabolic rewiring is a hallmark of DC activation as well as of dysfunctional DCs in the tumor microenvironment. Can the authors describe whether deficiency or inhibition of the PPP or STING pathways affects DC metabolism more broadly?
Response: We thank the reviewer for your valuable comments and have performed additional experiments to address this question. Wild-type BMDCs were cultured in vitro and treated with or without the PPP inhibitor 6-AN (50 µM), followed by metabolomic profiling. KEGG pathway analysis revealed that PPP inhibition broadly perturbs cellular metabolism, affecting pathways including amino acid metabolism (e.g., alanine, aspartate, and glutamate metabolism; arginine biosynthesis; glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism), fatty acid metabolism (e.g., glycerophospholipid metabolism; biosynthesis of unsaturated fatty acids), and central carbon metabolism (e.g., TCA cycle; one-carbon pool by folate). Collectively, these results indicate PPP inhibition triggers extensive metabolic reprogramming beyond the pathway itself.
Figure IX: PPP inhibition affects DC metabolism. KEGG pathways enrichment analysis of non-targeted metabolomics data of BMDCs treated with PPP inhibitor 6-AN (50 μM) or untreated (Ctrl). P values were calculated by Fisher’s exact test.
6. Is PPP deficiency in late-stage DCs due to limited glucose availability, and is the expression or activity of G6PD altered?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comments and have included additional experiments.
First, we measured intracellular glucose levels in early- and late-stage intratumoral cDCs from MC38 tumor-bearing wild-type mice using mass spectrometry. The results revealed no significant difference in glucose levels between the two stages (Supplemental Figure 3a). Similarly, glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) levels remained comparable between early- and late-stage cDCs (Supplemental Figure 3a).
Given the observed impairment in PPP activity in late-stage cDCs, we next examined the expression of key PPP enzymes. qPCR analysis showed that transcript levels of G6pdx and Pgd were both downregulated in late-stage cDCs (Supplemental Figure 3c). This finding was corroborated at the protein level by western blot, which confirmed reduced G6PDX expression (Supplemental Figure 3b). Since the first and rate-limiting step of the PPP involves the conversion of G6P to 6-phosphogluconolactone (6PGL) by G6PD, accompanied by R5P production, we further assessed downstream metabolites. Consistent with reduced G6PDX protein level, both 6PGL and R5P levels were lower in late-stage cDCs (Supplemental Figure 3a).
In summary, these results indicate that late-stage intratumoral cDCs exhibit diminished G6PDX expression and overall PPP metabolic flux.
7. Is treatment with a STING agonist alone sufficient to restore the function of late-stage DCs?
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s valuable suggestion and have included additional experiments. We isolated early- and late-stage tumor-infiltrating cDCs from MC38 tumor-bearing mice and treated late-stage cDCs with or without the STING agonist DMXAA in vitro for 12h. These cells were then subcutaneously injected adjacent to the tumors to wild-type MC38 tumor-bearing mice on day 3 and 6 post-tumor inoculation. Compared with untreated late-stage intratumoral cDCs, those receiving STING agonist treatment exhibited delayed tumor growth and enhanced T cell cytokine production, achieving functional levels comparable to early-stage intratumoral cDCs (Figure 4, n and o, and Supplemental Figure 6z). These results demonstrate that restoring STING signaling in late-stage intratumoral cDCs rescues their antitumor immunity. Furthermore, the findings confirm that impaired STING activity contributes to the dysfunctional state of late-stage intratumoral cDCs.
8. Could the authors clarify which DC subsets were included in the gating strategy for tumor-infiltrating DCs (Tu-DCs)? The current gating of CD45 CD24- F4/80 Ly6C CD11c MHCII cells may encompass both cDC1 and cDC2 populations. In addition, please specify the gating strategy used for Flt3L-derived BMDCs.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for your valuable feedback. In response to the comments, we have now included the gating strategy for tumor-infiltrating DCs in the revised manuscript (Supplementary Figure 1). Our gating strategy indicated that we isolated both intratumoral cDC1 and cDC2 subsets for our analyses and experiments. Additionally, we have added the corresponding gating strategy for Flt3L-induced BMDCs in the revised manuscript (Supplementary Figure 5a). Incorporating these revisions in response to the reviewer’s comments has significantly strengthened the manuscript.
Other comments:
1. Please provide more detailed information on the experimental procedures. In particular, the ratios and cell numbers used are not clearly described. For example: DC cell numbers used for Western blot analysis; The number of DCs transferred in adoptive transfer experiments (early vs. late DCs from tumors); The ratios and cell numbers of DCs and T cells used in co-culture experiments. These details are essential for reproducibility and should be revised accordingly.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this critical feedback, which is essential for ensuring the reproducibility of our work. We have thoroughly revised the Materials and Methods section, and Figure legends to provide comprehensive and precise experimental details as requested.
